## Correct chords, unclear arrangement

Every note can belong to the harmony and the result still comes out as porridge.
Put two voices in one pitch range, give them similar envelopes, leave them in
the same stereo position, and their identities blur. Turning one down moves the
balance and leaves both in the same congested region.

Three dimensions get you out. *Register* is pitch height. *Timbre* is the
spectral character separating a hollow sustained tone from a bright pluck. Space
covers stereo position and apparent depth. So move a part an octave, shorten its
envelope, pan it off its neighbour, or push it behind a drier foreground with
reverb.

Leave volume for last. Give each role a place where you can find its attacks,
then let amplitude decide which role stands forward.

## One skeleton, three treatments

Four chords get rendered three ways: sparse, dense, wide.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78

progression = [
  chord(:c3, :minor),
  chord(:ab2, :major),
  chord(:eb3, :major),
  chord(:bb2, :major)
]

define :render_skeleton do |chords, layout|
  chords.each do |notes|
    if layout == :sparse
      use_synth :piano
      play notes.first, release: 1.8, amp: 0.7
      play notes.last + 12, release: 1.2, amp: 0.6
    elsif layout == :dense
      use_synth :saw
      play_chord notes.map { |pitch| pitch + 12 }, release: 1.8, amp: 0.55
      play_chord notes.map { |pitch| pitch + 15 }, release: 1.8, amp: 0.5
    else
      with_fx :reverb, room: 0.7, mix: 0.35 do
        use_synth :hollow
        play notes.first, release: 2.4, amp: 0.55, pan: -0.5
      end
      use_synth :pluck
      play notes.last + 24, release: 0.7, amp: 0.65, pan: 0.55
    end
    sleep 2
  end
end

render_skeleton progression, :sparse
sleep 1
render_skeleton progression, :dense
sleep 1
render_skeleton progression, :wide
```

The dense pass stacks two saw voicings three semitones apart, piling related
spectra into one band. Can you still trace an individual tone through it? The
wide pass sends a long low sustain left and a short high pluck right, and it's
the one to compare everything else against.

## Collapse the separation on purpose

1. Drop `+ 24` from the wide layout's pluck. Its attacks fall back toward the
   sustained part's register while the pans stay put. Pan locates two sounds
   horizontally; it can't stop their spectra competing.
2. Restore the octave and set both pans to 0. Register and envelope still
   separate the centred parts. You're hearing how much clarity survives once
   stereo position stops helping.
3. Raise the reverb mix to 0.75. The sustained voice recedes and its attack
   loses its edge. Return to 0.35 before you touch anything else.

## Masking, and three ways around it

*Masking* is what happens when sounds occupy similar frequency bands at similar
times and make each other harder to perceive. Register separation thins the
overlap. Contrasting envelopes stop attacks and sustains competing continuously.
Panning supplies level and timing differences between your ears, and reverb
shifts the ratio of direct to reflected sound, which is what sets a source's
apparent distance.

They interact, which is why fixing one sometimes fixes nothing. Drop a saw's
fundamental and its upper partials stay where they were. A short release opens a
gap; a long reverb tail refills it. Depth is relational too: a reverberant voice
sounds distant because a drier voice gives you a foreground. Put every part in
the same big room and the whole image recedes together.

## Diagnose your own collisions

Arrange one eight-bar skeleton three ways without editing the chord data: two
roles sparse, four or more dense, and a wide version where every role differs
from its neighbour along two dimensions. For each collision you hear, write one
line naming the competing roles and the dimension they're fighting over. Fix it
without moving a chord root, and keep your hands off the master level.
